subChunks.title: var, Text Blocks & Pattern Matching instanceof
subChunks.hookHtml: Java has shed its verbose reputation. Since Java 10 and 15, three quality-of-life features — local variable type inference with var, multi-line text blocks, and pattern matching instanceof — make code cleaner without sacrificing type safety.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
var — Local Variable Type Inference

Introduced in Java 10, var lets the compiler infer the type of a local variable from its initialiser. The type is still static and fixed at compile time — it just doesn't need to be written twice.

// Without var
ArrayList<String> spells = new ArrayList<>();

// With var — same type, less repetition
var spells = new ArrayList<String>();
var count = spells.size(); // inferred as int

var limitations — you cannot use var for:

  • Fields
  • Method parameters
  • Return types
  • Variables without an initialiser
  • Lambda parameters (well, you can in Java 11+ but it's unusual)

Text Blocks

Text blocks (Java 15+) let you write multi-line strings naturally with """ delimiters. Leading indentation is stripped automatically based on the closing delimiter's position.

String spellDescription = """
        Name: Arcane Surge
        Power: 95
        Element: Arcane
        Effect: Unstoppable magical force
        """;
System.out.println(spellDescription);

The content between the opening """ and closing """ is the string. Escape sequences still work. Trailing newlines are included.

Pattern Matching instanceof

Before Java 16, you needed to cast explicitly after an instanceof check:

// Old way
if (obj instanceof String) {
    String s = (String) obj; // redundant cast
    System.out.println(s.length());
}

Pattern matching combines the check and binding into one expression:

// Modern way — Java 16+
if (obj instanceof String s) {
    System.out.println(s.length()); // s is already a String here
}

// Works in a method:
static void classify(Object obj) {
    if (obj instanceof String s) {
        System.out.println("It's a String: " + s);
    } else if (obj instanceof Integer n) {
        System.out.println("It's an Integer: " + n);
    } else {
        System.out.println("Unknown type");
    }
}

storyBeats.text: The Academy's ancient scribes had copied the same type twice on every scroll — once on the left, once on the right, an exhausting ritual. A young reformist mage had petitioned for change for decades. Java finally listened.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: When the type is obvious from the right side, var spares you the redundancy. But do not abuse it — if var hides intent, write the type. Clarity beats brevity.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Text blocks end the era of concatenated strings. A spell description belongs on multiple lines — let it breathe. The compiler strips the leading indentation so your code can be properly indented.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And pattern matching instanceof eliminates the dance of check-then-cast. One line, one step, the variable is bound and typed immediately.

storyBeats.speaker: Code

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Three tasks in main:

  1. var: Declare three variables using var: a List<String> with Arrays.asList("Fire", "Ice"), an int as the list's size, and a String via String.join(", ", list). Print each.
  2. Text block: Create a text block with at least two named lines (e.g., Name: Arcane Surge and Element: Arcane) and print it.
  3. Pattern matching: Write a static method classify(Object obj) that prints "It's a String: " + s if the obj is a String, or "It's an Integer: " + n if Integer. Call it from main with a String and an Integer argument.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what 'type inference' means for var — Java is still statically typed, so what exactly does the compiler do? Then explain why var cannot be used for method parameters, and what would go wrong if it could.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory: use var to declare a list of potion names and print its size. Write a text block with a potion label and effect on separate lines and print it. Write identify(Object obj) that prints "String detected: " + the value if String, or "Number detected: " + the value if Integer. Call it with both types.

Prints Number detected for an Integer argument

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The compiler's ability to deduce a type automatically from context. var uses this for local variables; generics also rely on type inference.
var cannot be used for fields, method parameters, return types, or variables without initialisers. It is strictly a local variable feature.
Java strips indentation from text blocks based on the least-indented line (or the closing delimiter), so you can indent the block with your code.
A Java 16 feature where instanceof both checks and casts in one expression: if (obj instanceof String s) gives you s as a String directly.
The new variable introduced by a pattern match (the s in 'instanceof String s'). It is in scope within the true branch of the if statement.
Java 21 allows patterns with a 'when' guard: case String s when s.length() > 5 — combining pattern binding with a condition.
The formal process by which Java features are proposed, refined, and delivered. var was JEP 286, text blocks JEP 378, pattern matching instanceof JEP 394.

questions.questionHtml: Which of these is a valid use of var?
questions.explanationHtml: var requires an initialiser on the same line so the compiler can infer the type. It cannot be used for fields (private var), return types, or without an initialiser. var items = new ArrayList<String>(); is valid — the type is inferred as ArrayList<String>.
"Hello" matches instanceof String s, and "Hello".length() is 5. The integer 7 matches instanceof Integer n, and 7 * 2 = 14.

questions.correctAnswer: var requires an initialiser on the same declaration line so the compiler can infer the type. Split declaration and assignment is not allowed. Fix: var message = "Hello, Academy!";
questions.explanationHtml: var uses the initialiser expression to determine the type at compile time. If no initialiser is present on the declaration line, there is nothing to infer from, and the code fails to compile. Combine the declaration and assignment: var message = "Hello, Academy!";

questions.questionHtml: When should you prefer writing the explicit type instead of var?
options: Always — var reduces readability in all cases
When the right-hand side clearly shows the type (e.g., new ArrayList<>())
When the type is not obvious from the initialiser and a reader needs to know it
questions.correctAnswer: When the type is not obvious from the initialiser and a reader needs to know it
questions.explanationHtml: var works best when the type is evident from context. When a method returns an opaque type (e.g., var result = processSpells(data)), the reader loses information. In that case, writing the explicit type aids comprehension. The guiding question is: does hiding the type hurt the reader?

subChunks.title: Sealed Classes & Switch Pattern Matching
subChunks.hookHtml: What if the compiler could guarantee you've handled every possible subtype of an interface — the same way it guarantees you've handled every enum constant? Sealed classes make that possible, and pattern matching instanceof ties the pieces together.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Sealed Interfaces and Classes

A sealed interface (Java 17) restricts which classes may implement it. The permits clause lists every allowed implementor — no others are possible.

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Triangle {}

record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {}
record Square(double side) implements Shape {}
record Triangle(double base, double height) implements Shape {}

Because the compiler knows the exact set of subtypes, it can verify exhaustive handling — just like enums in a switch.

Pattern Matching with if-instanceof (Java 17 Compatible)

In Java 17, you can use chained instanceof pattern matching to dispatch on sealed subtypes:

static String describe(Shape s) {
    if (s instanceof Circle c) {
        return "Circle with radius: " + c.radius();
    } else if (s instanceof Square sq) {
        return "Square with side: " + sq.side();
    } else if (s instanceof Triangle t) {
        return "Triangle base: " + t.base();
    } else {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Unknown shape");
    }
}

Switch Expressions with Pattern Matching (Java 21)

Java 21 (and Java 17 with --enable-preview) allows switch expressions over sealed types with pattern cases. The compiler enforces exhaustiveness.

// Java 21 style — shown for reference
String result = switch (s) {
    case Circle c    -> "Circle radius: " + c.radius();
    case Square sq   -> "Square side: " + sq.side();
    case Triangle t  -> "Triangle base: " + t.base();
}; // no default needed — sealed is exhaustive

Since the sandbox runs Java 17, use the if-instanceof style shown above for exercises.

Why Sealed Classes?

  • Express domain hierarchies that are intentionally closed
  • Enable exhaustive analysis by the compiler (and IDEs)
  • Pair naturally with records for algebraic data types
  • Prevent accidental extension from unrelated code

Sealed Hierarchy Rules

  • Every permitted subtype must be in the same package (or module)
  • Subtypes must be final, sealed, or non-sealed
  • Records are implicitly final, so they work perfectly as permitted types

storyBeats.text: The Academy's Shape Taxonomy had grown unruly — foreign scholars kept adding new shapes that the Core Spells weren't prepared to handle. Eldrin sealed the hierarchy, granting the compiler the authority to enforce it.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A sealed interface is a closed contract. You declare exactly which forms it may take. No outsider can slip in an unlisted subtype and break your handling code.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: In Java 17, chain your instanceof pattern matches. The sealed contract is your promise that no else branch will ever be reached for a well-formed Shape.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: In Java 21, the switch expression elevates this further — the compiler itself verifies exhaustiveness over sealed types, and the else is gone. Your code reads like the algebra it models.

storyBeats.speaker: Code

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
At the top of your file (outside Main), define:

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {}
record Square(double side) implements Shape {}

Inside Main, write a static method describe(Shape s) that uses chained instanceof pattern matching:

  • If Circle: return or print "Circle with radius: " + the radius
  • If Square: return or print "Square with side: " + the side

In main, call describe(new Circle(5.0)) and describe(new Square(3.0)) and print the results.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what 'sealed' means in Java and why it is valuable beyond just good documentation. How does sealing a hierarchy change what the compiler can verify? Contrast with a regular interface that anyone can implement.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory: define a sealed interface Spell permits Offensive, Defensive with record Offensive(String name, int power) and record Defensive(String name, int shield). Write a cast(Spell s) method using instanceof pattern matching that prints "Attacking with [name] power [power]" for Offensive and "Defending with [name] shield [shield]" for Defensive. Call it with both types.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A Java 17 feature where a class or interface restricts which types may extend or implement it using the 'permits' clause.
A type defined as one of a fixed set of variants, common in functional languages. Sealed interfaces + records approximate ADTs in Java.
A switch expression where the compiler verifies that all possible values are handled — required for enums and (in Java 21) sealed hierarchies.
A modifier for a permitted subtype that reopens it for arbitrary extension, creating a mixed hierarchy of sealed and open branches.
A switch expression that can match on types and destructure records directly, with compiler-enforced exhaustiveness over sealed types.
Java 21 allows destructuring a record directly in a pattern: case Circle(double r) instead of case Circle c — then using c.radius().
The idea of using a switch to simultaneously check a type AND extract its components, enabled by combining sealed classes with record patterns.

questions.questionHtml: What does the permits clause in a sealed interface declaration specify?
options: The exact set of classes allowed to implement the interface
The module the interface belongs to
questions.correctAnswer: The exact set of classes allowed to implement the interface
questions.explanationHtml: permits lists every class (or interface) that is allowed to implement (or extend) the sealed type. No other class may implement it — the compiler enforces this at compile time.

questions.correctAnswer:
Woof from Rex
Meow from Luna
questions.explanationHtml: greet(new Dog("Rex")) matches the first instanceof branch, returning "Woof from Rex". greet(new Cat("Luna")) matches the second, returning "Meow from Luna".

questions.questionHtml: What is wrong with this sealed hierarchy?
questions.correctAnswer: Square is not listed in the permits clause of Shape, so it is not allowed to implement Shape. Add Square to the permits list: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
questions.explanationHtml: Every implementor of a sealed interface must appear in the permits clause. Square implements Shape is a compile error because Square is not permitted. Fix: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}

questions.questionHtml: You are modelling JSON values: a value is either a JsonString, JsonNumber, JsonBoolean, JsonNull, JsonArray, or JsonObject — nothing else. Which design is most appropriate?
options: A regular interface that any class can implement
An abstract class with six concrete subclasses
A sealed interface with six permitted record implementations
questions.correctAnswer: A sealed interface with six permitted record implementations
questions.explanationHtml: The set of JSON value types is fixed and closed — exactly the use case for a sealed interface. Each variant is a data carrier (ideal for records). The sealed hierarchy enables exhaustive handling in switch expressions and documents clearly that no other variants exist.
